problems.description: Naming violations across the created modules (measured convention score 0.67, 9 violations): celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py use non-PascalCase classes, a non-snake_case function, and module-level constants that are not UPPER_CASE.

Public function signatures lost their type hints (create_task(title) / get_task(task_id) / update_task(task_id, title=None, status=None)) versus the seed's create_task(title: str) -> dict, regressing API clarity.

init_db() now runs at module import time, so importing app.py writes tasks.db to the filesystem as a side effect before any request; the test fixture's DATABASE monkeypatch occurs after import has already touched the default DB.
Discrepancy with measurements: app.py and test_app.py are flagged 'Classes should use PascalCase' but neither file defines any classes — this flag appears to be a static-analyzer false positive.

strengths: Fixes a latent correctness bug: create_task previously inserted status='done' while returning 'pending'; it now relies on the DB default so state is consistent (AST +11 functions, smells -2).
Replaces deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc).
Removes dead code (legacy _legacy_format_date, unused _notify_admin stub, fetch_task alias) and an unused import.
Adds proper 400-level validation for payload type and title/status values, plus an explicit 404 for missing tasks on PUT.
Adds a pytest suite (test_app.py, 66 lines) with tmp_path/monkeypatch DB isolation.
Modernizes Flask routing (@app.get/@app.post/@app.put) and uses explicit column lists with a stable id DESC tiebreak in ordering.
Respects existing structure: same module layout, function names, and get_db() context-manager pattern.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive greenfield refactor that fixes a status bug, removes dead code, and adds validation and tests while respecting the existing Flask structure, though it sheds public type hints and leaves naming-convention violations (0.67) in the new modules.

problems.description: Hand-rolled HS256 JWT (create_token/decode_token) instead of an established library like PyJWT. The implementation is defensively correct (hmac.compare_digest, strict header/payload checks, broad exception handling), but a default JWT_SECRET of secrets.token_hex(32) generated at boot means tokens invalidate on every restart and would diverge across multi-process deployments — a latent auth-failure hazard (matches SonarQube smells +3 / cognitive complexity +20).
Migration leaves legacy tasks with NULL owner_id, and get_tasks/get_task now filter WHERE owner_id = ?, so pre-existing rows become invisible with no backfill or default-ownership strategy.
No test additions for the security-critical auth surface (register/login/require_auth, owner-scoped queries); +377 lines of new logic shipped with no coverage delta.
Inline schema evolution (ALTER TABLE + PRAGMA foreign_keys) embedded in init_db adds migration drift risk versus a versioned migration approach.

Convention score 0.67 with 9 naming violations (Classes PascalCase, Functions snake_case, Module constants UPPER_CASE) across app.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py. Flag: the supplied diff shows only app.py, so most violations fall outside the visible diff — either the commit touched more files than shown or the linter is scoring pre-existing code.

strengths: Consistent owner_id scoping on every task query (get_tasks/get_task/update_task) gives defense-in-depth against cross-user access (IDOR).

Defensively correct auth plumbing: constant-time signature comparison, explicit 400/401/409 status codes, werkzeug password hashing, and a require_auth decorator that cleanly composes with existing Flask patterns.
Zero new bugs and zero duplications per SonarQube, with all new imports limited to stdlib plus already-present Flask/werkzeug.
Adds an index on owner_id and enables foreign_keys, a sound schema direction for the multi-user model.
Reuses the existing get_db() context-manager pattern and matches the codebase's function-style structure rather than introducing new frameworks.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, correctly-implemented authentication feature that improves the app (owner-scoped queries, no new bugs), but carries notable technical debt from a hand-rolled JWT, a NULL-owner migration gap, and zero auth test coverage, with convention adherence at the measured 0.67.

problems.description: celery_config.py defines module-level constants `broker_url` and `result_backend` in lowercase; the codebase precedent (`DATABASE = os.environ.get(...)` in app.py) and the naming convention require UPPER_CASE. This is the one genuine diff-attributable convention violation.

app.py calls `send_notification_email.delay(g.current_user["username"], task["title"])`, passing a username into the parameter named `user_email` (notification_tasks.py:5). The task and tests assert on "alice" as if it were an email — a semantic mismatch. Either rename the param to `user_identifier` or resolve an actual email address.

Discrepancy with measurements: the 9 reported violations include 'Classes should use PascalCase' on app.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, and test_app.py despite the AST diff adding +0 classes, plus a violation on repositories.py which is NOT part of this commit's diff (+2 files only). These flags are scanner false positives / pre-existing code, not real defects introduced here.

Notification payload uses the user's username as the recipient identifier because the schema has no email column. Pragmatic given the spec's mock-only email requirement, but the spec signature says `send_notification_email(user_email, task_title)`.

strengths: Implements the Session 3 spec exactly: Celery task with the requested signature, celery_config.py with broker URL, result backend, and task routes, and async triggering from PUT /tasks/{id}.
Correct transition-only semantics: enqueues only when status actually changes to 'completed', so repeated PUTs to completed do not emit duplicate notifications.
Non-blocking via .delay() keeps the API response fast, and tests mock `delay` so the suite needs no running Redis and stays deterministic.
Existing endpoints, auth, and prior tests are untouched; new tests reuse the established client/auth_headers fixture style.
Broker URL and result backend are overridable via CELERY_BROKER_URL / CELERY_RESULT_BACKEND env vars.
commit_reviews.summary: Strong architectural fit and correct async-notification semantics, but the mechanical 0.67 convention score is inflated by scanner false positives (PascalCase flags with +0 classes added) and a pre-existing file (repositories.py), leaving the only genuine diff-attributable convention issue as the lowercase module constants in celery_config.py.

problems.description: BaseRepository's generic get_by_id/get_all/update/delete bypass the owner_id scoping the original app deliberately enforced everywhere (WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?). These unscoped methods are a latent authorization footgun for a multi-user API; only the custom owner-scoped methods are currently wired, but the base CRUD invites future misuse.

create/update assemble table and column names into SQL via f-strings. Table names come from class attrs and columns are validated against self.fields (mitigating injection), but runtime string interpolation of schema names is fragile vs. explicit SQL.

Schema management (initialize_database) is coupled into the data-access base class rather than a dedicated schema/migration concern; init_db() becoming a thin passthrough pushes DDL ownership into the repository layer.

Mechanical convention score 0.67; the new repositories.py adds a module-level constants UPPER_CASE violation. Most other flagged violations (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, test_app.py) are pre-existing and untouched by this diff, so the commit's own delta is modest.
task_repository()/user_repository() reconstruct a repository per call; stateless so harmless, but cognitive complexity rose +7 from the generic base logic and this could be module-level singletons.

strengths: Clean separation of data access from request handlers with a shared ABC contract, consolidating duplicated SQL from app.py.
-90 net lines; repeated INSERT/UPDATE/SELECT scaffolding replaced with one validated code path.
All wired routes use owner-scoped methods (create_for_owner/get_for_owner/update_for_owner), preserving the authorization invariant where it matters.
Parameterized queries retained throughout; no SQL-injection surface introduced.
New code follows naming conventions (PascalCase classes, snake_case functions) and internal consistency.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound, net-positive layering refactor that removes ~90 lines of duplicated SQL behind an ownership-safe repository layer, at the cost of a generic unscoped CRUD base that is a latent authorization footgun and a modest +7 cognitive complexity bump.

problems.description: rate_limit_key decodes the JWT (a DB identity lookup via decode_token) on every request before require_auth runs, duplicating auth work and adding a query per request even for endpoints that do not need it.
get_page_for_owner issues COUNT(*) on every page request, an O(n) scan that partially defeats the scalability benefit of cursor pagination for large task tables.
The test fixture mutates flask-limiter private internals (limiter._storage, limiter._limiter) to swap in MemoryStorage — brittle coupling to upstream internals that will break on library upgrades.
Changing the GET /tasks response shape from a bare array to {data, next_cursor, total} is a breaking API contract change; acceptable in a story app but should be versioned or documented.

Measured convention score (0.67) and 9 violations understate this commit: 5 of 9 violations are in files untouched by this diff (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py), and the AST shows +0 classes, so the PascalCase/constant complaints are pre-existing, not introduced here.

strengths: Keyset (cursor) pagination over OFFSET, correctly ordering on (created_at DESC, id DESC) with a matching composite index that supports the ORDER BY.
Tie-handling cursor logic re-fetches the cursor row's (created_at, id), keeping pages consistent under concurrent inserts.
Solid input validation (limit/cursor typing, positive bounds, cap at 100) with a parametrized test covering invalid inputs and a clean 400 response.
Rate limiting integrated idiomatically: config-block pattern with env-overridable storage URI, authenticated-user/IP key derivation, and a dedicated 429 JSON error handler.
Layered architecture respected — route delegates to repository via the established connection_factory pattern; snake_case naming and existing dict-return convention maintained.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-architected commit that cleanly adds keyset pagination and rate limiting with correct indexing and thorough tests; the measured 0.67 convention score is misleading since most violations are pre-existing in files this commit never touched.

compounding_issues: Session 2's hand-rolled HS256 JWT with a boot-time random secret invalidates tokens on every restart and diverges across processes; this forced Session 5's rate_limit_key to re-decode the JWT on every request, duplicating auth work before require_auth runs.

Session 2's inline ALTER TABLE migration left legacy tasks with NULL owner_id and no backfill or default-ownership strategy, so pre-existing rows became invisible once owner-scoped queries were enforced — a gap never repaired in later sessions.

Session 4's generic BaseRepository exposes unscoped get_by_id/get_all/update/delete that bypass the owner_id scoping established in Session 2 as the security boundary, a latent authorization footgun in a multi-user API.
Session 2's schema had no email column, so Session 3 passed the username into the send_notification_email(user_email) parameter — a semantic mismatch that persisted as the only working design.
Security-critical auth surface (register/login/require_auth, owner-scoping) shipped in Session 2 with zero test coverage (+377 lines, no test delta) and stayed untested through Session 5.
Convention debt was never paid down: the measured convention score stayed flat at 0.673 across all five sessions (lowercase module constants, missing type hints shed in Session 1).
Session 1's init_db() runs at module import time, writing tasks.db as an import side effect and constraining test isolation for every later session.
key_decisions: Session 1 full rewrite of the seed: fixed the status-mismatch bug, deleted legacy helpers, added validation and tests — establishing the single-file Flask architecture, but dropping public type hints.
Session 2 hand-rolled HS256 JWT (hmac + base64, no PyJWT) with a per-boot random secret, plus owner-scoped task queries — the security architecture that everything downstream built on.
Session 2 inline schema evolution (ALTER TABLE + PRAGMA foreign_keys inside init_db) instead of versioned migrations — making future schema changes ad-hoc.
Session 3 Celery + Redis-backed async email notifications (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py) — introduced the Redis dependency that Session 5's Flask-Limiter storage reuses.
Session 4 Repository pattern with an abstract BaseRepository providing generic CRUD while routes go through owner-scoped methods — decoupled data access but seeded the unscoped-CRUD footgun.

Session 5 keyset (cursor) pagination with a composite (owner_id, created_at, id) index plus Flask-Limiter at 100 req/min/user — cleanly cross-cutting, but changed GET /tasks from a bare array to {data, next_cursor, total}, a breaking API contract change.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically: the test suite grew 8 → 23 → 25 → 25 → 34 passing with zero SonarQube bugs across all commits, every session review returned 'better', and the codebase matured from a flat single-file script into a properly layered app (routes → repositories → async task workers) with auth, pagination, and rate limiting. However the arc was accretive rather than debt-reducing: cognitive complexity climbed steadily (8 → 20 → 2 → 7 → 16), the convention score never moved off 0.673, and debt seeded in Session 2 (hand-rolled JWT, NULL-owner migration gap, untested auth) propagated forward — forcing the username-as-email workaround in Session 3 and the redundant per-request JWT decode in Session 5. Each session built correctly on the prior one, but early architectural shortcuts constrained later options rather than being paid down.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session build where a capable agent grew a buggy one-file seed into a layered, fully-tested task-management API, with strong integration between sessions but steadily accruing — never paid-down — security and convention debt seeded by the Session 2 auth architecture.
